questions.title: Threats and measures
questions.text: Match each threat to the measure that best protects against it.

left.text: A hacker tries to connect to the school server from the Internet
A laptop containing pupils' data is stolen
One hard disk in the server fails
A power cut in the server room

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–Firewall, L2–Encryption, L3–Mirroring, L4–UPS. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Prevent hacking
questions.text: List **three** security measures to prevent hacking.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any three (1 each): biometric; access control / access rights; antivirus; firewall; double / two-factor authentication; strong password; intranet; encryption; software updates
[max 3] Accept any correct answer
scheme.model_answer: 1 Firewall. 2 Two-factor authentication. 3 Strong passwords.

questions.title: Physical risks
questions.text: Complete the table with **one** countermeasure for each physical risk to a server room.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Theft (1): locked room / key cards / biometric entry / CCTV / guards
Fire (1): smoke detectors / gas fire-suppression / fireproof safe for backups / off-site backup
Power cut (1): UPS / back-up generator
Overheating (1): air conditioning / temperature monitoring / ventilation
scheme.model_answer: Theft: key-card lock on the door. Fire: gas fire-suppression system. Power cut: UPS. Overheating: air conditioning.

questions.title: Purpose of a UPS
questions.text: Explain the purpose of an **uninterruptible power supply (UPS)** for a server.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A battery keeps the server running for a short time when the mains power fails (1)
- so data can be saved / the server shut down safely / generator started, preventing data loss or damage (1)

points.criterion: Battery power during a power cut

scheme.model_answer: Its battery keeps the server running for a few minutes when the power fails, so data can be saved and the server shut down safely without losing data.

questions.title: How a firewall works
questions.text: Describe how a **firewall** protects a network.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): monitors / checks data packets entering and leaving the network; compares them with a set of security rules (IP addresses, ports); blocks unauthorised / suspicious packets / connections; logs attempted attacks; can block certain websites
scheme.model_answer: It checks every data packet going in and out of the network against a set of rules, such as allowed IP addresses and ports, and blocks any packet that breaks the rules.

questions.title: Firewall and viruses
questions.text: A firewall scans the files on a hard disk and removes any viruses it finds.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Removing viruses from files is the job of anti-virus software; a firewall filters network traffic.

questions.title: Encryption
questions.text: Describe how **encryption** protects data.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Data (plaintext) is scrambled into ciphertext using an algorithm and a key (1)
- so if it is intercepted / stolen it cannot be understood without the key (1)
scheme.model_answer: Encryption scrambles the data into ciphertext using a key, so anyone who intercepts or steals it cannot read it without the correct key.

questions.title: Symmetric or asymmetric
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

prefill: The same key is used to encrypt and decrypt
A public key encrypts and a private key decrypts
The key has to be shared secretly with the receiver

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Symmetric (1); 2 Asymmetric (1); 3 Symmetric (1)

questions.title: What encryption does not do
questions.text: A company encrypts all files on its laptops. Which statement is correct?

options.content: The laptops can no longer be stolen
A thief who steals a laptop cannot read the files without the key
The files can no longer be deleted

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: Encryption makes stolen data unreadable; it does not prevent theft, deletion or malware.

questions.title: Biometric methods
questions.text: Select **two** biometric authentication methods.

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Biometrics: advantage and disadvantage
questions.text: State **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of using fingerprint recognition to log in to a computer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantage (1): unique / hard to copy; cannot be forgotten, lost or shared; fast and convenient
Disadvantage (1): expensive hardware; false rejection (dirty / cut finger) / false acceptance; privacy — data cannot be changed if stolen
scheme.model_answer: Advantage: a fingerprint cannot be forgotten or shared like a password. Disadvantage: it may be rejected if the finger is dirty or cut.

questions.title: Two-factor authentication
questions.text: Explain how **two-factor authentication** makes an online bank account more secure.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The user must provide two different types of evidence, e.g. a password and a code sent to the phone / a fingerprint (1)
- so a hacker who steals / guesses the password still cannot log in without the second factor (1)

points.criterion: Stolen password alone is not enough

scheme.model_answer: After the password, the bank also asks for a one-time code sent to the customer's phone, so a hacker who has stolen the password still cannot log in without the phone.

questions.title: How anti-virus detects malware
questions.text: Describe **two** methods anti-virus software uses to detect malware.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): signature-based — compares files with a database of known virus signatures; heuristic / behaviour analysis — detects suspicious behaviour of programs; real-time scanning of files as they are opened / downloaded
scheme.model_answer: 1 It compares files with a database of signatures of known viruses. 2 It watches for suspicious behaviour, such as a program changing many system files, to catch new viruses.

questions.title: Virus countermeasures
questions.text: State **two** countermeasures, other than installing anti-virus software, that reduce the risk of a computer virus infection.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): keep OS / software updated; do not open unknown attachments / links; scan / disable autorun for USB drives; download only from trusted sources; firewall; limited user accounts; user training; regular backups
scheme.model_answer: 1 Keep the operating system updated. 2 Do not open e-mail attachments from unknown senders.

questions.title: Data backup
questions.text: Describe what is meant by a **data backup**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A copy of the data made on a separate medium / location (1)
- so it can be restored if the original is lost / damaged / deleted (1)
scheme.model_answer: A copy of data stored on a separate medium, ideally in another place, so it can be restored if the original data is lost or damaged.

questions.title: Types of backup
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the type of backup described.

prefill: Copies all the data every time
Copies only data changed since the last backup of any type
Copies all data changed since the last full backup

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Full (1); 2 Incremental (1); 3 Differential (1)

questions.title: Off-site backups
questions.text: Explain why backups should be kept **off-site** (in a different building or in the cloud).

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A fire / flood / theft at the main site would destroy both the original and a backup kept in the same place (1)
- an off-site copy survives, so the data can still be restored (1)

points.criterion: Disaster at one site destroys both

scheme.model_answer: If the building burns down or is flooded, a backup kept in the same room would be destroyed with the original; an off-site copy survives and the data can be restored.

questions.title: Disk mirroring
questions.text: Describe how **disk mirroring** protects data.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Data is written to two (or more) disks at the same time, so they hold identical copies (RAID 1) (1)
- if one disk fails, the system continues from the other disk without data loss / downtime (1)
scheme.model_answer: Every piece of data is written to two disks at the same time, so if one disk fails, the computer keeps working from the identical copy on the other disk.

questions.title: Mirroring vs backup
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether the statement describes **backup** or **disk mirroring**.

prefill: Copies data continuously, in real time
Can be used to restore a file deleted by mistake last week
The system keeps working with no downtime when a disk fails
A copy can be stored in another city

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Mirroring (1); 2 Backup (1); 3 Mirroring (1); 4 Backup (1)

questions.title: Ransomware attack
questions.text:
A small accounting firm stores clients' data on one server with disk mirroring. Last month ransomware encrypted all its files.

Discuss why disk mirroring did not protect the data, and recommend measures the firm should take.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 4 marks:
- Mirroring copies every change immediately, so the encrypted files were written to both disks (1)
- mirroring only protects against disk failure, not malware / deletion (1)
- Regular backups, at least one offline / off-site, to restore unencrypted files (1)
- Anti-virus updated / firewall / OS updates (1)
- Staff training on phishing / not opening attachments; limited user rights (1)
[Max 4]
scheme.model_answer: Disk mirroring writes every change to both disks at once, so when the ransomware encrypted the files, both copies were encrypted; mirroring only protects against a disk failing. The firm should make regular backups and keep one copy offline or off-site so it can restore the original files, install and update anti-virus software and a firewall, keep the system updated, and train staff not to open suspicious attachments.

questions.title: A protection plan for a school
questions.text:
A school stores pupils' personal data and marks on a server connected to the Internet. Teachers take laptops home.

Evaluate the measures the school should use to protect this data. Refer to physical security, firewalls, encryption, biometrics or passwords, anti-virus software, backup and disk mirroring.

scheme.mark_scheme:
One mark per well-explained measure linked to the scenario (max 5), e.g.
- locked server room / UPS / fire protection (physical)
- firewall to block Internet attacks on the server
- encryption of laptops so stolen laptops do not expose data
- strong passwords + 2FA / biometrics for staff log-in, access rights so pupils cannot see marks
- anti-virus with updates against malware
- regular off-site / cloud backups to restore after loss or ransomware
- disk mirroring so the server keeps running if a disk fails
Evaluation / conclusion (1): e.g. no single measure is enough; mirroring is not a backup; cost vs risk
scheme.model_answer: The server should be in a locked room with a UPS, so it cannot be stolen or damaged by a power cut. A firewall should block unauthorised connections from the Internet. Teachers' laptops should be encrypted, so if one is stolen the pupils' data cannot be read. Staff should log in with strong passwords and two-factor authentication, and access rights should stop pupils from seeing marks. Anti-virus software must be kept updated. The server should use disk mirroring so it keeps running if a disk fails, but because mirroring copies deletions and ransomware too, the school also needs regular backups stored off-site. No single measure is enough, so the school should combine them.

questions.title: Protecting a school network
questions.text: A school's server stores pupils' personal data and is connected to the Internet. Teachers also keep pupils' marks on their laptops.

parts.title: Three measures
parts.text: List **three** security measures to prevent hacking.

scheme.mark_scheme: Biometric (1) Access control (1) Antivirus (1) Firewall (1) Use double authentication (1) Use strong password (1) Intranet (1) Encryption (1) [max 3] Accept any correct answer
scheme.model_answer: 1 Firewall. 2 Strong passwords. 3 Two-factor authentication.

parts.title: Firewall
parts.text: Describe how a firewall protects the school server.

scheme.mark_scheme: Checks / monitors packets entering and leaving the network (1); against security rules — IP addresses / ports (1); blocks unauthorised traffic (1) [Max 2]
scheme.model_answer: It checks each packet coming from the Internet against security rules and blocks any connection that is not allowed.

parts.title: Firewall limitation
parts.text: State **one** threat that a firewall cannot protect against.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): virus on a USB stick / in an allowed e-mail attachment; insider / authorised user misusing data; phishing; physical theft; disk failure
scheme.model_answer: A virus brought in on a USB stick.

parts.title: Encryption
parts.text: Explain how encryption protects the pupils' marks if a teacher's laptop is stolen.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The data is scrambled with a key / stored as ciphertext (1)
- the thief cannot read / understand the marks without the key (1)
scheme.model_answer: The marks are stored as ciphertext, so the thief cannot read them without the decryption key.

questions.title: Authentication and malware
questions.text: A bank wants to make its staff log-in and computers more secure.

parts.title: Biometric methods
parts.text: State **two** biometric methods the bank could use.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): fingerprint; face recognition; iris / retina scan; voice recognition; hand geometry; signature dynamics
scheme.model_answer: 1 Fingerprint recognition. 2 Iris scan.

parts.title: Biometrics evaluated
parts.text: State **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of biometrics compared with passwords.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantage (1): unique / hard to copy; cannot be forgotten or shared; faster
Disadvantage (1): expensive; false rejections / acceptances; cannot be changed if stolen / privacy
scheme.model_answer: Advantage: it cannot be forgotten or given to another person. Disadvantage: if the biometric data is stolen it cannot be changed like a password.

parts.title: Two-factor authentication
parts.text: Explain how two-factor authentication improves security.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Two different types of evidence are needed (something you know / have / are) (1)
- a stolen password alone is not enough to log in (1)
scheme.model_answer: Staff need a password and also a fingerprint or a code on their phone, so someone who has stolen a password still cannot log in.

parts.title: New viruses
parts.text: Explain how anti-virus software can detect a **new** virus that is not yet in its signature database.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Heuristic / behaviour-based detection (1)
- watches for suspicious actions, e.g. changing system files / copying itself / encrypting many files, and quarantines the program (1)
scheme.model_answer: It uses heuristic analysis: it watches what programs do and blocks one that behaves suspiciously, such as trying to change many system files.

questions.title: The server room
questions.text: A hospital's server room holds the servers with patients' records.

parts.title: Physical risks
parts.text: Draw a line to link each physical risk to the most suitable countermeasure.

right.text: Door opened only by key card and CCTV

scheme.mark_scheme: Theft–R1, Fire–R2, Overheating–R3. One mark per correct line.

parts.title: UPS
parts.text: Explain why the hospital's servers are connected to a UPS.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Battery power keeps the servers running when the mains power fails (1)
- so records are not lost / servers shut down safely / generator can start; patient records remain available (1)
scheme.model_answer: If the power fails, the UPS battery keeps the servers running until the generator starts, so patient records are not lost or damaged.

parts.title: Off-site backup
parts.text: Explain why the hospital keeps a copy of its backups in another building.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A fire / flood / theft could destroy the servers and any backups in the same room (1)
- the copy in another building survives, so records can be restored (1)
scheme.model_answer: A fire in the server room would destroy both the servers and any backups stored there; a copy in another building can still be used to restore the records.

questions.title: Backup and disk mirroring
questions.text: An online shop uses disk mirroring on its web server and also makes backups.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Data is written to two disks simultaneously / identical copies (1)
- if one disk fails the other is used and the system keeps running (1)
scheme.model_answer: All data is written to two disks at the same time, so if one fails the server keeps running from the other one.

parts.title: Why also backup
parts.text: Explain why the shop also needs backups, even though it uses disk mirroring.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Deletions / corruption / ransomware are copied to both disks immediately (1)
- backups keep earlier copies that can be restored / can be off-site in case of fire or theft (1)
scheme.model_answer: If a file is deleted or encrypted by ransomware, the change is mirrored to both disks at once, so only a backup lets the shop restore an earlier, undamaged copy.

parts.title: Full vs incremental
parts.text: Compare a **full** backup with an **incremental** backup.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each), both sides: full copies all data vs incremental only changes since the last backup; full slower / more space vs incremental faster / less space; full easier / faster to restore vs incremental needs full + every incremental
scheme.model_answer: A full backup copies all the data each time, while an incremental backup copies only what has changed since the last backup, so it is faster and uses less space; however, restoring needs the full backup plus every incremental one.

parts.title: Off-site medium
parts.text: State **one** suitable medium or service for keeping an off-site backup.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): cloud storage; magnetic tape stored elsewhere; external hard disk kept in another building; remote server / data centre
scheme.model_answer: Cloud storage.

summary: Measures that protect data and computer systems — protection against physical risks, firewalls (inter-network screens), encryption, biometrics and anti-virus countermeasures — and using data backup and disk mirroring (RAID 1) to keep data safe.

blocks.content: Data and computer systems are at risk from **people** (hackers, thieves, careless users), **malicious software** and **physical events** (fire, flood, power cuts, hardware failure). No single measure protects against everything, so organisations use **several layers of protection** ("defence in depth").

blocks.title: Threats and the measures that protect against them
rows: Fire, flood, power cut, theft of hardware
**Physical security**, UPS, fire-suppression systems, **backup** stored off-site
Interception of data in transit, stolen laptops

blocks.title: Physical risks and countermeasures
rows: Locked server rooms, security guards, CCTV, cable locks, entry by key card or biometrics, visitor logs
Smoke detectors, gas-based fire-suppression systems (no water near computers), fireproof safes for backups
Servers not in basements, raised floors, water sensors
**Uninterruptible power supply (UPS)**, surge protectors, back-up generators
Air conditioning, temperature monitoring in server rooms
Disk mirroring (RAID), spare parts, regular maintenance
No food or drink near computers, protective cases, user training

blocks.content: A device with a **battery** that keeps computers running for a short time when the mains power fails, so that work can be **saved** and the system **shut down safely** (or a generator started).

Hardware or software that **monitors all data packets passing between a private network (or computer) and the outside network (Internet)** and **allows or blocks** them according to a set of **security rules**. It is the "screen" between two networks.

flowchart TB
  I[Internet] <--> F{Firewall: check each packet against the rules}
  F <--> N[School network: servers and PCs]
  F -. blocked .-> X[Unauthorised connection]
blocks.caption: A firewall sits between the internal network and the Internet

items.title: What a firewall does
items.content:
- Checks the **source and destination IP address**, **port number** and protocol of every packet.
- **Blocks** packets that do not match the rules (e.g. connections to unused ports, known bad addresses).
- Can **block access** to certain websites or applications.
- **Logs** attempts to connect, so attacks can be investigated.
- Can hide the internal addresses of the network from outsiders.

items.title: Limitations
items.content:
- Cannot stop malware that arrives through **allowed** channels (e-mail attachments, USB sticks).
- Does not protect against **insiders** already inside the network.
- Must be **configured correctly** — bad rules either block useful traffic or let attacks through.

blocks.content: Converting data (**plaintext**) into an unreadable form (**ciphertext**) using an **algorithm** and a **key**, so that only someone with the correct key can **decrypt** it and read it. Encryption does **not** stop data being stolen, but makes stolen data **useless** to the thief.

flowchart TB
  P[Plaintext: Exam on Monday] -->|encrypt with key| C[Ciphertext: Q8#k2!zP...]
  C -->|send over the Internet| C2[Ciphertext received]
  C2 -->|decrypt with key| P2[Plaintext: Exam on Monday]
blocks.caption: Encrypting and decrypting a message

blocks.title: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption
rows: A **public key** encrypts, a **private key** decrypts
Solves key sharing — the public key can be given to anyone

items.title: Where encryption is used
items.content:
- **HTTPS / SSL / TLS** — web pages, online banking, payments.
- **Full-disk encryption** on laptops and phones, encrypted USB drives.
- **Wi-Fi** (WPA2 / WPA3).
- Messaging apps with end-to-end encryption.
- Storing **passwords** as hashes (one-way) rather than plain text.

items.title: Advantages and disadvantages
items.content:
- ✔ Stolen or intercepted data cannot be read.
- ✔ Protects data on lost devices.
- ✘ If the **key is lost**, the data is lost too.
- ✘ Takes processing time; does not stop deletion or ransomware.

blocks.content: Authentication using **unique physical or behavioural characteristics** of a person, which are compared with a stored **template**. Examples: **fingerprint**, **face recognition**, **iris / retina scan**, **voice recognition**, **hand geometry**, **signature dynamics**.

blocks.title: Biometric methods
rows: Sensor reads the ridges of a finger
Cheap, fast; dirty or cut fingers can fail
Contactless; lighting, glasses or masks can affect it
Camera scans the pattern of the eye
Very accurate; expensive; some users dislike it
A cold or background noise can cause rejection

items.title: Advantages
items.content:
- Characteristics are **unique** and hard to **copy or guess**.
- **Cannot be forgotten, lost or shared** like a password or card.
- Fast and convenient to use.
- Gives an **audit trail** of exactly who entered.

items.title: Disadvantages
items.content:
- **Expensive** hardware.
- **False rejections** (an authorised user is refused) and **false acceptances**.
- **Privacy** concerns — biometric data is personal; if stolen it **cannot be changed** like a password.
- Some characteristics change (injury, age).

blocks.title: Two-factor authentication (2FA)
blocks.content: Combining **two different types** of evidence — something you **know** (password), something you **have** (phone, card) and something you **are** (biometric) — makes unauthorised access much harder. Example: a password plus a code sent to your phone.
A utility program that **scans** files, e-mails, downloads and memory to **detect, quarantine and remove malware** (viruses, worms, Trojans, spyware, ransomware).

blocks.title: How anti-virus software works
items: **Signature-based detection** — compares files with a database of known malware **signatures**; the database must be **updated** regularly.
**Heuristic / behaviour analysis** — detects **suspicious behaviour** (e.g. a program trying to change many system files), so it can catch new malware.
**Real-time (on-access) scanning** checks files as they are opened or downloaded.
Infected files are **quarantined** (isolated) or **deleted**; the user is warned.

blocks.title: Other virus countermeasures
rows: Fixes security holes that malware uses
Many viruses spread by e-mail and phishing
Scan **USB drives** before use; disable autorun
Malware cannot easily spread or change the system
Files can be restored after ransomware
People recognise phishing and suspicious files

blocks.content: A **copy of data** stored on a **separate medium**, preferably in a **different location**, so that the original can be **restored** if it is lost, damaged, deleted, stolen or encrypted by ransomware.

blocks.title: Types of backup
rows: Only data changed **since the last backup of any type**
Slowest — the full backup **plus every** incremental one
Data changed **since the last full** backup

items.title: A good backup strategy
items.content:
- Back up **regularly** and **automatically** (e.g. every night), at a time when the system is not busy.
- **3-2-1 rule:** keep **3** copies of the data, on **2** different types of media, with **1** copy **off-site** (or in the cloud).
- Keep at least one copy **offline**, so ransomware cannot encrypt it.
- **Encrypt** backups and keep them physically secure.
- **Test** restoring from the backup regularly.

items.title: Backup media
items.content:
- External hard disks / SSDs.
- Magnetic **tape** (cheap for very large amounts, used by companies).
- **Cloud storage** — off-site automatically; needs an Internet connection.
- Network-attached storage (NAS).

blocks.content: Data is written to **two (or more) disks at the same time**, so that every disk holds an **identical copy**. If one disk **fails**, the system **continues working** from the other disk **without losing data or stopping**.

write "file.docx"
                      |
              +-------+-------+
              |               |
        +-----------+   +-----------+
        |  Disk 1   |   |  Disk 2   |
        | file.docx |   | file.docx |     identical copies
        +-----------+   +-----------+
   Disk 1 fails  ->  the server keeps running from Disk 2
blocks.caption: Disk mirroring: every write goes to both disks

blocks.title: Backup vs disk mirroring
rows: Deletion, corruption, ransomware, fire, theft (if off-site), disk failure
Data is **restored** — some downtime; changes since the last backup are lost
Yes — you can go back to an earlier copy
No — a deletion or virus is **copied to both disks instantly**
Needs at least **double** the disk space

blocks.content: If a file is **deleted**, **corrupted** or **encrypted by ransomware**, the change is mirrored to **both** disks at once. Organisations therefore use **both**: mirroring for **availability** and backups for **recovery**.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: List three security measures to prevent hacking. [3]**
Firewall (1); strong passwords / two-factor authentication (1); biometrics / access control / anti-virus / encryption (1).

**Q: Describe how a firewall protects a school network. [2]**
It checks every **data packet** entering and leaving the network against **security rules** (1) and **blocks** packets from unauthorised sources / to unused ports (1).

**Q: Explain why a company should use both disk mirroring and backup. [2]**
Mirroring keeps the system **running without data loss if a disk fails** (1), but a deletion or virus is copied to both disks, so a **backup** is needed to **restore earlier, undamaged copies** (1).

**Q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using fingerprints to log in. [2]**
Advantage: fingerprints are **unique** and **cannot be forgotten or shared** (1). Disadvantage: **false rejections** if the finger is dirty or cut / biometric data cannot be changed if stolen (1).

- Saying a firewall **removes viruses** — that is anti-virus software; a firewall **filters network traffic**.
- Saying encryption **stops data being stolen** — it makes stolen data **unreadable**.
- Treating disk mirroring as a backup (see above).
- Keeping the backup **in the same room** as the original — a fire destroys both.
- Giving vague answers such as "use security" — name the **specific** measure and **what it does**.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: Name four physical risks and a countermeasure for each.
Describe what a firewall checks and what it cannot protect against.
What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
Give two advantages and two disadvantages of biometrics.
Explain signature-based and heuristic virus detection.
Compare full, incremental and differential backups.
Explain how disk mirroring works and why it does not replace backups.

topic_exam.title: Data protection measures — Exam (Paper 1 style)
topic_exam.instructions: Answer **all** questions. The number of marks is given in brackets [ ] at the end of each part. Total: 30 marks. Time: 40 minutes.
